items.stem: In a market economy, how are resources allocated?
options: Through the price mechanism, by the decisions of consumers and producers
items.answer: Through the price mechanism, by the decisions of consumers and producers
items.markingKey: Market economy: private ownership, price mechanism, consumer sovereignty.

items.stem: Explain how the price mechanism allocates resources in a market economy.
items.answer: Changes in demand and supply change prices; higher prices signal scarcity and raise profits, giving firms an incentive to move resources into that market, while falling prices cause resources to leave. Prices also ration goods to those willing and able to pay.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price changes as signal; 1 mark: incentive/profit; 1 mark: reallocation of resources/rationing [3]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of a market economy.
items.answer: Efficiency: competition and the profit motive encourage low costs and innovation. Choice: consumer sovereignty means firms produce what consumers want. Also: no costly planning bureaucracy; quick response to change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each advantage, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: In Quentara, private firms produce most goods, but the government provides healthcare and education and regulates monopolies. Which type of economic system does this describe?
items.answer: Mixed economy
items.markingKey: Mixed economy: both the price mechanism and government allocate resources.

items.stem: In Esteria, private firms produce most goods, but the government provides healthcare and education and regulates monopolies. Which type of economic system does this describe? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Mixed economy: both the price mechanism and government allocate resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mixed economy; 1 mark: explanation – both the price mechanism and government allocate resources. [2]

items.stem: Identify the economic system described in each case and explain your answer. (i) In Lunaria, the state owns all land and factories and workers are directed to jobs by government agencies. (ii) In Lunaria, prices are set by supply and demand and almost all firms are privately owned.
items.answer: (i) Planned economy (ii) Market economy
items.markingKey: (i) Planned economy – state ownership and direction of factors. [2] (ii) Market economy – resources are allocated by the price mechanism with private ownership. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Pelora was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 1.5% to 5.0%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.22 to 0.35, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) State the type of economic system that Pelora has now. Give a reason. (b) Explain why inequality may have increased.
items.answer: (a) Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. (b) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. [2] (b) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Gorvania was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 1.5% to 5.0%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.28 to 0.42, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) State the type of economic system that Gorvania has now. Give a reason. (b) Explain why growth may have increased after the reforms.
items.answer: (a) Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. (b) Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. [2] (b) Credit: Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. [3]

items.stem: What is meant by consumer sovereignty?
options: The government protects consumers from firms
Consumers own the firms that produce goods
Consumers set the prices of goods
Consumers’ spending decisions determine what is produced
items.answer: Consumers’ spending decisions determine what is produced
items.markingKey: Consumers “vote” with their spending; firms respond to profit signals.

items.stem: Explain why a pure market economy may lead to an unequal distribution of income.
items.answer: Incomes depend on ownership of factors and their market value; those with valuable skills or wealth earn much more, and there is no government redistribution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: incomes reflect factor ownership/market value; 1 mark: no redistribution [2]

items.stem: Explain why a market economy in Rovania might fail to provide enough street lighting.
items.answer: Street lighting is a public good: non-excludable, so consumers can free ride; firms cannot charge for it, so there is no profit incentive to supply it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: public good/free rider; 1 mark: no profit incentive [2]

items.stem: In Korvia, the price of printed books rose from $80 to $96 and sales rose from 5 to 8 thousand units, while demand for petrol scooters fell. The average cost of producing printed books stayed at $68 per unit. Calculate the percentage increase in the price of printed books.
Calvania has recently removed price controls on most goods. Explain how the price mechanism allocates resources in a market economy.
items.answer: Signalling, incentive and rationing functions; demand/supply changes change prices and profits; resources move; consumer sovereignty; diagram of a demand shift.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Signalling, incentive and rationing functions; demand/supply changes change prices and profits; resources move; consumer sovereignty; diagram of a demand shift. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Sundara was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 1.5% to 5.0%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.25 to 0.38, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the Gini coefficient. (b) Explain why inequality may have increased.
items.answer: (a) 52% (b) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting.
items.markingKey: (a) (0.38 − 0.25)/0.25 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2]

items.stem: Gorvania has recently removed price controls on most goods. Assess whether a market economy is the best way to allocate scarce resources.
items.answer: For: Efficiency, innovation, choice, quick response to change, no costly planning. Against: Market failure: public goods, externalities, merit/demerit goods, inequality, monopoly power, information failure; government intervention needed; mixed economy. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Efficiency, innovation, choice, quick response to change, no costly planning. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Market failure: public goods, externalities, merit/demerit goods, inequality, monopoly power, information failure; government intervention needed; mixed economy. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: In a planned economy, who decides what to produce?
items.answer: The state (government planners)
items.markingKey: Central planning; state ownership of resources.

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of a planned economy.
items.answer: Lack of incentives (no profit motive) leads to low efficiency and innovation; planners lack information so produce the wrong goods, causing shortages and surpluses; little consumer choice; large bureaucracy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each disadvantage, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why a planned economy might achieve lower unemployment than a market economy.
items.answer: The state directs workers into jobs and sets output targets regardless of demand, so jobs are guaranteed even when they are not efficient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: state allocates jobs; 1 mark: not dependent on market demand [2]

items.stem: Planners in Pelora set the price of refrigerators below the market level. At this price 300 thousand households want to buy refrigerators each year, but the plan provides only 200 thousand. Calculate the shortage as a percentage of the quantity supplied.
In Selmaria, the state owns all land and factories and workers are directed to jobs by government agencies. Which type of economic system does this describe? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Planned economy: state ownership and direction of factors.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Planned economy; 1 mark: explanation – state ownership and direction of factors. [2]

items.stem: Which is an advantage claimed for a planned economy?
options: A more equal distribution of income
Prices that respond quickly to demand
items.answer: A more equal distribution of income
items.markingKey: Planners can prioritise basic needs and equality.

items.stem: Explain how shortages arise when prices are fixed by planners.
items.answer: If the fixed price is below the price at which demand equals supply, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, leading to queues, rationing and black markets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price below equilibrium; 1 mark: excess demand/queues [2]

items.stem: Planners in Zentara set the price of refrigerators below the market level. At this price 500 thousand households want to buy refrigerators each year, but the plan provides only 250 thousand. Calculate the shortage as a percentage of the quantity supplied.

Identify the economic system described in each case and explain your answer. (i) In Korvia, most shops and farms are private, but the state runs the railways and pays unemployment benefits. (ii) In Korvia, a rise in the price of concert tickets quickly attracts new private firms into the industry with no government involvement.
items.answer: (i) Mixed economy (ii) Market economy
items.markingKey: (i) Mixed economy – a combination of private and public sectors. [2] (ii) Market economy – price signals and the profit motive guide resource allocation. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: What is a mixed economy?
options: An economy with both rich and poor people
An economy that produces both goods and services
An economy in which resources are allocated partly by the price mechanism and partly by the government
An economy that trades with many countries
items.answer: An economy in which resources are allocated partly by the price mechanism and partly by the government
items.markingKey: Mixed: private and public sectors coexist.

items.stem: Explain two problems that may occur when a planned economy changes to a market economy.
items.answer: Unemployment as inefficient state firms close; inflation as price controls end; rising inequality; lack of legal and financial institutions (property rights, banks); corruption in privatisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each problem, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why governments in mixed economies provide some goods and services directly.
items.answer: Public goods would not be provided by the market; merit goods would be under-consumed; equity of access to health and education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: market failure reason; 1 mark: equity reason [2]

items.stem: In Tarvia, the state owns all land and factories and workers are directed to jobs by government agencies. Which type of economic system does this describe?
items.answer: Planned economy
items.markingKey: Planned economy: state ownership and direction of factors.

items.stem: In Ostrelia, prices are set by supply and demand and almost all firms are privately owned. Which type of economic system does this describe? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Market economy: resources are allocated by the price mechanism with private ownership.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Market economy; 1 mark: explanation – resources are allocated by the price mechanism with private ownership. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Umbria Nova was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. items.answer: (a) 50% (b) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting.
items.markingKey: (a) (0.42 − 0.28)/0.28 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the balance between the public and private sectors differs between mixed economies.
items.answer: It reflects political values and choices about the role of the state, the extent of market failure and views on equity versus efficiency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: political/normative choices; 1 mark: market failure/equity [2]

items.stem: The government of Quentara privatises its state-owned brewing company. Explain one possible benefit and one possible cost.
items.answer: Benefit: profit motive raises efficiency and investment. Cost: a private monopoly may raise prices or cut unprofitable services; job losses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefit; 1 mark: cost [2]

items.stem: Quentara began moving from a planned to a market economy in Year 1. : State sector share of output (%), Unemployment rate (%), Inflation (%); Year 1: 90, 3, 3; Year 5: 55, 11, 25. By how many percentage points did the state sector’s share of output fall?
items.answer: 35 percentage points

items.stem: Identify the economic system described in each case and explain your answer. (ii) In Rovania, a central planning office decides how many tractors, flats and tonnes of steel are produced each year. (iii) In Rovania, a rise in the price of fresh fruit quickly attracts new private firms into the industry with no government involvement.
items.answer: (i) Mixed economy (ii) Planned economy (iii) Market economy
items.markingKey: (i) Mixed economy – a combination of private and public sectors. [2] (ii) Planned economy – the state allocates resources through planning targets. [2] (iii) Market economy – price signals and the profit motive guide resource allocation. [2] Total [6]

items.stem: Which is a feature of a market economy?
items.answer: Private ownership of most resources
items.markingKey: Private property rights and the profit motive.

items.stem: Explain why a market economy in Jovania might fail to provide enough street lighting.
items.answer: Street lighting is a public good: non-excludable, so consumers can free ride; firms cannot charge for it, so there is no profit incentive to supply it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: public good/free rider; 1 mark: no profit incentive [2]

items.stem: Demand for electric cars in Umbria Nova rises sharply. Explain how the price mechanism reallocates resources in a market economy.
items.answer: Price of electric cars rises; producers’ profits rise, so they expand output and new firms enter, attracting labour and capital from less profitable industries such as petrol cars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price rises; 1 mark: profit incentive; 1 mark: resources move [3]

items.stem: In Ostrelia, the price of petrol scooters rose from $12 to $15 and sales rose from 10 to 14 thousand units, while demand for e-books fell. The average cost of producing petrol scooters stayed at $9.60 per unit. Calculate the percentage increase in the price of petrol scooters.
In Ostrelia, a rise in the price of smartphones quickly attracts new private firms into the industry with no government involvement. Which type of economic system does this describe?
items.answer: Market economy
items.markingKey: Market economy: price signals and the profit motive guide resource allocation.

items.stem: Which problem is often found in planned economies?
options: High unemployment from the trade cycle
Shortages and queues for many consumer goods
items.answer: Shortages and queues for many consumer goods
items.markingKey: Prices fixed below market levels; poor information for planners.

items.stem: Explain why the government of Ostrelia, a planned economy, may find it easier to build large infrastructure projects than a market economy.
items.answer: The state controls resources directly and can direct labour and capital to priority projects without needing profit or private finance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direct control; 1 mark: no profit requirement [2]

items.stem: Planners in Halvoria set a target for factories to produce a fixed weight of nails each month. Explain why this might result in goods that consumers do not want.
items.answer: Factories meet the weight target by making a few very heavy nails rather than the sizes consumers need, because targets reward quantity rather than usefulness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: targets not linked to demand; 1 mark: mismatch [2]

items.stem: Planners in Jovania set the price of washing machines below the market level. At this price 640 thousand households want to buy washing machines each year, but the plan provides only 400 thousand. Calculate the shortage as a percentage of the quantity supplied.

items.answer: (a) 120 thousand units. (b) Queuing (first come, first served), waiting lists, rationing by allocation or vouchers, priority by need; consequence: black markets selling at higher prices, or time wasted queuing.

items.stem: Which is a problem commonly faced by an economy in transition from planned to market?
options: Government spending rises to 100% of GDP
Prices fall sharply as controls are removed
Unemployment rises as inefficient state firms close
items.answer: Unemployment rises as inefficient state firms close
items.markingKey: Transition: unemployment, inflation when prices are freed, inequality, weak institutions.

items.stem: Samuel wrote in a homework answer: ‘Moving to a market economy always makes everyone better off immediately.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Transition often brings unemployment, inflation and inequality in the short run; gains in efficiency and choice take time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Transition often brings unemployment, inflation and inequality in the short run; gains in efficiency and choice take time. [2]

items.stem: Dravonia is moving from a planned to a market economy. Explain why unemployment may rise in the first few years.
items.answer: Inefficient state firms lose subsidies and face competition, so many close or cut jobs; new private firms take time to grow; workers lack the skills new firms need.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: closure of inefficient state firms; 1 mark: slow growth of private sector/skills mismatch [2]

items.stem: What happens in a market economy when demand for a good rises?
options: Its price rises, signalling firms to move resources into producing it
The government orders more to be produced
items.answer: Its price rises, signalling firms to move resources into producing it
items.markingKey: Higher price → higher profit → resources reallocated.

options: Managers have weak incentives to cut costs or innovate
items.answer: Managers have weak incentives to cut costs or innovate

items.answer: Without competition and the profit motive firms have weak incentives to cut costs or innovate, so they tend to be less efficient.

However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.28 to 0.42, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) Explain why growth may have increased after the reforms. (b) Explain why inequality may have increased.
items.answer: (a) Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. (b) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Profit motive and competition raise efficiency and innovation; resources move to where they are most valued; FDI attracted. [3] (b) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2]

items.stem: Why does inflation often rise during transition to a market economy?
options: Price controls are removed and prices rise to market levels
items.answer: Price controls are removed and prices rise to market levels
items.markingKey: Previously suppressed prices adjust upwards.

items.stem: The government of Nordavia privatises its state-owned coffee shop company. Explain one possible benefit and one possible cost.
items.answer: Benefit: profit motive raises efficiency and investment. Cost: a private monopoly may raise prices or cut unprofitable services; job losses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefit; 1 mark: cost [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Arjun wrote: ‘A mixed economy is one that produces both agricultural and manufactured goods.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A mixed economy is one where resources are allocated partly by the market and partly by the government.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A mixed economy is one where resources are allocated partly by the market and partly by the government. [2]

items.stem: Marvona began moving from a planned to a market economy in Year 1. : State sector share of output (%), Unemployment rate (%), Inflation (%); Year 1: 90, 1.5, 2; Year 5: 55, 8, 18. By how many percentage points did the state sector’s share of output fall?
items.answer: 35 percentage points

items.stem: Selmaria began moving from a planned to a market economy in Year 1. : State sector share of output (%), Unemployment rate (%), Inflation (%); Year 1: 70, 3, 2; Year 5: 35, 11, 18. (a) Calculate the percentage fall in the state sector’s share of output. (b) Using the data, explain two problems of transition. (c) Suggest why these problems might be temporary.
items.answer: (a) 50% (b) Unemployment rose from 3% to 11% as state firms closed; inflation rose from 2% to 18% as price controls ended. (c) New private firms expand and absorb workers; once prices reach market levels, inflation falls; institutions develop.
items.markingKey: (a) (70 − 35)/70 × 100 [1] (b) each problem with data [2] (c) reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Twenty years ago Nordavia was a centrally planned economy. Since reforms began, most state firms have been privatised and prices are set by markets. Average annual growth has risen from 2.0% to 6.5%, and shops now offer a wide choice of goods. However, the Gini coefficient has risen from 0.25 to 0.38, and the government still runs schools, hospitals and the railway. (a) State the type of economic system that Nordavia has now. Give a reason. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in the Gini coefficient. (c) Explain why inequality may have increased.
items.answer: (a) Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. (b) 52% (c) Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Mixed economy: markets allocate most resources, but the state provides schools, hospitals and railways. [2] (b) (0.38 − 0.25)/0.25 × 100 [2] (c) Credit: Incomes now reflect the market value of skills and ownership of capital; privatisation transferred wealth; less state wage-setting. [2]
